<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Homebound older adults (≥60 y) and their informal family caregivers face multiple challenges in meeting their instrumental, emotional, and informational needs, which result in lower functional status, multiple comorbidities, and poorer mental health. Caregivers are tasked with providing uncompensated care for medically complex older adults, often without formal health care training. This circumstance may translate to high levels of burden and greater vulnerability to social isolation and loneliness, which may precipitate chronic stress and compromise caregiver health. In recent years, numerous health-focused technologies assisting with health-promoting behaviors such as physical activity, stress management, and nutritional tracking have emerged. However, little is known about how these tools are adopted by family caregivers of homebound older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This descriptive qualitative study aimed to explore how caregivers of homebound older adults perceive technology in the context of supporting caregiving and aging in place through focus groups and one-on-one interviews.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a descriptive qualitative study using in-person and online video conference focus group methodology with 40 individuals (32 caregivers, 6 clinicians, and 2 additional key informants) to explore perspectives on caregivers’ use of technology to support their caregiving activities. Participants completed a brief sociodemographic questionnaire prior to all interviews. Procedures for thematic analysis were used to analyze the data and identify emerging themes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Three main themes (and related subthemes) emerged from the data: (1) these technologies are not designed for people like us, (2) balancing the scales, and (3) preserving a sense of self. Caregivers’ experiences with technology are marked by a paradox: the same technologies that can ease caregiving activities may also impose new burdens through additional costs, uncertainty, learning demands, and emotional strain.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Caregivers should not navigate these technological tensions alone. Realizing the promise of technology requires more than innovative tools—it demands caregiver-centered design, accessible and equitable implementation strategies, and sustained clinical and health system support to ensure that technology alleviates, rather than amplifies, caregiver burden.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Barriers and Facilitators to Technology Use Among Caregivers of Homebound Older Adults: Descriptive Qualitative Study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>There is limited evidence on the patterns of health care use among older adults in Singapore over the past decade.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines whether the proportion of specific services used within sociodemographic subgroups, the factors associated with health care use, and the network structure of health care use have changed over a decade.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We used data from 2 repeated nationwide cross-sectional surveys of Singapore residents aged 60 years and older, conducted in 2013 (n=2565) and 2023 (n=2010). Health care service use was obtained from an adapted version of the Client Service Receipt Inventory and analyzed using multivariable logistic regression and network analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The most significant changes between 2013 and 2023 were in the proportions of older adults who had consulted private hospital/clinic doctors (decreased by 4.6 percentage points; n=655, 26.5% vs n=425, 21.9%;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.02), consulted public and private dentists (increased by 6.4 percentage points; n=215, 11.6% vs n=269, 18%;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001), and had health insurance (increased by 26.9 percentage points; n=1312, 59.9% vs n=1697, 86.8%;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001). Those diagnosed with high blood pressure and diabetes were more likely to consult primary care doctors, while those diagnosed with dementia and heart problems were more likely to consult public hospital doctors and health workers, visit emergency departments, and require hospitalization services in both 2013 and 2023. We also found that those diagnosed with dementia were more likely to visit intermediate and long-term care services in both 2013 and 2023. Network analysis revealed that there were strong connections between respite care, nursing homes, and hospital admissions in 2023.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study provides important data on population-level changes in health care usage among older adults across the decade from 2013 to 2023, which will help policymakers ensure better health care delivery for older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Changes in Patterns of Health Care Use Among Older Adults in Singapore Across a Decade: Repeated Nationwide Cross-Sectional Survey

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The increasing life expectancy provides an opportunity for healthy longevity, but frailty is a potential challenge. Existing studies of frailty prevalence in England are largely cross-sectional, use heterogeneous frailty definitions, and rarely break down population-level drivers or project future burden, limiting their use for health and social care planning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to explore temporal trends of frailty prevalence and project scenario-based future prevalence up to 2040 for the community-dwelling population aged 50 years and older in England.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Prevalence of frailty (measured using a frailty index) in the overall sample and subgroups of age, sex, educational level, and marital status from 2002 to 2022 was estimated among the community-dwelling population aged 50 years and older using 10 waves of nationally representative data from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA; n=6226 to 11,218 across waves). The number of individuals with frailty was also derived in each year. Joinpoint regression models were used to explore temporal trends of frailty prevalence. A linear probability regression model was performed using pooled data from 10 waves of the ELSA to explore driving factors and project future prevalence. Decomposition analysis was used to estimate the contribution of individual factors to the change in prevalence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      A statistically nonsignificant (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.61) increase of 2.3 percentage points from 15.5% (1738/11,218) in 2002 to 17.8% (1108/6226) in 2022 was observed, with the number of individuals with frailty growing from 2,560,122 to 3,791,038 among community-dwelling adults aged 50 years and older in England. Those with advanced age, who were female, had a lower educational level, and/or were single had a consistently higher prevalence of frailty. Opposing contributions netted to this overall change: improvements in sociodemographic conditions and educational attainment and healthier lifestyle behaviors offset 222.5%, 94.9%, and 51.6% of the observed increase, respectively. Under scenario-based projections, prevalence was estimated at 20.5% (95% CI 19.2%-21.9%) in 2040, corresponding to 5,213,689 people with frailty.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Despite a modest increase in prevalence among the community-dwelling population aged 50 years and older, the substantial growth in the absolute number of individuals with frailty indicates a likely rise in future care demands. The study contributes a 20-year trend, decomposition, and forecast framework for community-dwelling older adults. Findings support prioritizing broader sociodemographic development alongside educational attainment and healthy lifestyles, with potential policy approaches including income and social protection, housing improvements, access to health care, and prevention. Key limitations include self-reported measures, exclusion of care home residents, and potential influence of unmeasured effects.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Temporal Trends in the Prevalence of Frailty in England From 2002 to 2022, With Forecasts to 2040: Longitudinal Secondary Analysis of a National Cohort Study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Physical inactivity accelerates functional decline in rural older adults with limited exercise resources. Although bodyweight training is scalable, whether benefits depend on professional supervision remains unclear. We compared professional- and trained volunteer-led bodyweight training programs (BWTP) on functional fitness and body composition in rural community-dwelling older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this quasi-experimental, community-based, three-group pretest-posttest study with community-level allocation (April 2021-January 2022), adults aged ≥65 years who were independent in activities of daily living and not engaged in other regular exercise programs were assigned to a professional trainer, trained volunteer, or comparison group. The intervention groups received a 12-week BWTP. Functional fitness and body composition were assessed pre- and postintervention, and Group × Time effects were examined using two-way mixed ANOVA.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among 72 participants (Professional Trainer Group, PTG, n = 25; Volunteer Trainer Group, VTG, n = 22; Comparison Group, CG, n = 25), several functional fitness outcomes showed significant Group × Time interactions (p ≤ .003; partial η² = .155-.248). Both intervention groups improved mobility and postural stability more than the CG. PTG improved handgrip strength versus CG (Hedges’ g = 0.85), whereas VTG showed the largest lower-limb muscular endurance gain (g = 1.26). CG declined in several functional measures. No body-composition outcome remained significant after adjustment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Trained volunteer-led BWTP may extend exercise delivery and support functional fitness in resource-limited rural communities. Hybrid models with professional oversight warrant evaluation because body-composition effects did not persist after multiplicity adjustment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Effects of professional trainer-led and trained volunteer-led bodyweight training programs on physical fitness and body composition of rural community-dwelling older adults

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cognitive frailty (CF), the co-occurrence of physical frailty and cognitive impairment without dementia, is a potentially reversible condition associated with adverse outcomes in older adults. However, heterogeneity in operational definitions and measurement approaches limits comparability and clinical translation. This review examined how CF has been defined and operationalized, including adaptations to established criteria.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>PubMed, Web of Science, and PsycINFO were searched for English-language studies published from 2013 through 2025. Eligible studies explicitly referred to CF in adults aged 50 years or older. Risk of bias was assessed using Joanna Briggs Institute tools. Definitions, assessment tools, thresholds, and operational criteria were synthesized descriptively. Fried Phenotype (FP) implementation was examined using an adaptation-equivalence typology classifying domain-level measurement and threshold deviations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among 257 studies, 13 frailty and 26 cognitive assessment tools were identified. The FP was predominantly utilized (n = 164/257; 64%), although 68% (n = 112/164) modified the measurement method, threshold, or both in at least one domain. The Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) thresholds used to define cognitive impairment varied substantially, whereas all studies using the Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) used a threshold of 0.5. Dementia was not explicitly excluded in 50 studies, despite its exclusion being a defining criterion of CF.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>CF remains operationally heterogeneous. Updated international consensus and minimum reporting standards are needed to clarify core criteria and acceptable adaptations. FP-based studies should explicitly report domain-level modifications to improve comparability, reproducibility, and evidence synthesis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Operationalizing Cognitive Frailty: A Systematic Review of Definitions, Tools, and Measurement Inconsistencies

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Narrative approaches to quality improvement are increasingly adopted by long-term care organizations to gain insight into quality from the perspectives of older persons. However, it remains unclear how organizations experience the organizational challenges of embedding these approaches in new quality improvement routines and policies. This study aims to investigate what tensions arise when organizing and embedding narrative approaches and how organizations respond to these tensions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>An exploratory qualitative multiple-method design consisting of observations, semi-structured interviews and document analysis was used. Data were collected in Dutch nursing homes between February 2024 and June 2025. To gain in-depth and broader insights, organizations were observed for a longer period (n = 2) and interviews were conducted with other organizations (n = 9) about organizing a narrative approach.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>: Four tensions were identified: 1) steering on pre-determined themes vs. emergent themes from experiences 2) abstracting narratives into broad quality terms vs. preserving the richness of narratives; 3) organizing quality top-down and in silos vs. as a collaborative and dynamic process; and 4) accounting for compliance vs. learning for improvement.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The tensions show that organizing a narrative process goes beyond organizational challenges, but requires a paradigm shift in how organizations view and organize quality improvement. It requires a different way of data collection, analysis and collaboration and emphasizes relationality and learning over individualized accounting. When organizations get stuck between two different quality paradigms, this can lead to several risks. The implications, risks and potential of narrative approaches are discussed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Shifting paradigms: key tensions in putting the person’s narrative central in improving quality of care in Dutch nursing homes

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Socioeconomic inequalities in depressive symptoms are well documented, yet little is known about how these inequalities unfold during midlife and whether they vary across national and historical contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using harmonized longitudinal data spanning 1992 to 2022 from 16 countries (United States, England, France, Austria, Belgium, Germany, Switzerland, Israel, Italy, Spain, Greece, Denmark, Netherlands, Sweden, South Korea, and China), this study modeled trajectories of depressive symptoms among adults aged 45 to 65 across four wealth-based socioeconomic strata: Low (1st to 15th percentile), Lower-middle (16th to 45th), Upper-middle (46th to 75th), and High (76th to 100th).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Results revealed cross-national disparities: midlife adults in the United States reported higher depressive symptoms than their peers in most other nations, and this difference was most pronounced among lower SES groups. In most nations, later-born cohorts reported more depressive symptoms, with Upper-middle SES individuals exhibiting the largest historical increases. Beyond these mean-level patterns, lower SES groups were found to exhibit greater heterogeneity across three trajectory features of depressive symptoms (i.e., mean-levels at age 50 as well as linear and quadratic changes in depressive symptoms). This may suggest that under socioeconomic disadvantage, depressive symptoms are less tightly structured by SES alone and more strongly shaped by other contextual and individual factors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Collectively, findings highlight that mental health inequalities in midlife are deeply embedded in societal and historically changing structures. Policies that strengthen social protections and promote economic security may reduce these disparities and enhance well-being across the life course.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Psychological costs of low wealth in midlife: Lower socioeconomic status carries greater disadvantage for depressive symptoms in the United States than Europe and China

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study investigates how the growing population of older Americans living alone adapts to daily life, testing three sociological hypotheses regarding “upsides” to solo living: spending more time outside, spending more time with non-residential ties, and spending more time in organized activities. We also consider whether such adaptations are unequal, investigating potential fault lines across key social categories including race/ethnicity, education, gender, and disability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using 2003–2019 American Time Use Survey data (N = 83,997), we employed multiple regression analysis to estimate both the likelihood of participation and the duration of time spent in each of these ways.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Results support the notion of locational and social adaptation: older adults living alone spend significantly more time outside the home and more time with friends and non-residential family than their co-resident peers. However, we found that solo dwellers spend less time in organized activities. Consistent with one dimension of the unequal adaptation hypothesis, several behavioral patterns were stratified by race/ethnicity, with Black older adults standing out from each of the other groups.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings point to living alone as a distinct social ecology rather than a simple marker of deficit, with older adults adapting through the reorganization of daily exposure to people and places. This adaptation does not appear strongly structured by most social categories, though strong racialized differences suggest that future research should continue to assess the way diverse older Americans live together and with others.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Finding the upsides to living alone: Adaptation and inequality among older U.S. adults?

                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study explores the relationship between marital status, living arrangements, and aging well among Chinese adults aged 50 and older.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using data from the China Family Panel Studies (CFPS), we developed a multidimensional measure of aging well (physiological, functional, cognitive, psychological, and subjective). Analysis was based on a five-category typology of marital and living arrangements.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A clear hierarchy emerged in the findings: married individuals co-residing with spouses experienced the most favorable outcomes, while unmarried individuals living alone faced the greatest challenges. Non-traditional arrangements (e.g., married living apart) also showed significant difficulties, particularly in subjective well-being. These associations were moderated by socio-demographic factors, with disparities being less pronounced among respondents aged 75+, retirees, urban residents, and those with healthier lifestyles.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings underscore the enduring importance of co-resident marital relationships while highlighting the evolving influence of diverse family arrangements on the well-being of older adults in China.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Marital Status, Living Arrangement, and Aging Well in China

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Parental longevity is linked to better offspring cognition, with limited evidence from middle-income countries. We examined associations between parental longevity and cognition in Mexico while controlling for health, socioeconomic status (SES), and genetic factors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We used the 2018 wave of the Mexican Health and Aging Study (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">n</jats:italic>
                      = 5,049; age 65+). Maternal/paternal longevity was based on survival to age 85 or older. We used latent variable regressions to estimate associations with offspring cognition, adjusting for demographics, parental characteristics, health, health behaviors, SES, and APOE-ε4 carrier status.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>About 31% of respondents had a mother and 31% had a father who survived to age 85 or older. Maternal, but not paternal, longevity was independently associated with better offspring cognition. The maternal association persisted after full adjustment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Maternal longevity was positively linked to offspring cognition independent of health, health behaviors, SES, and APOE-ε4. Intergenerational support and broader genetic factors may contribute to this association.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To examine the association between early-life circumstances and healthy aging among community-dwelling older Chinese adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data were from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study. We used regression methods to identify independent and joint associations of six early-life factors with healthy aging as assessed by the Chinese Healthy Aging Index (CHAI; 0–12), a composite score evaluating six physiological systems.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Of 3,069 participants, 4.82% had the healthiest CHAI score (0–2). After multivariable adjustment, personal education and family economic status were associated with healthier CHAI individually; the cumulative early-life score was associated with the CHAI, both dichotomously and continuously. Each additional score was associated with 37% (95% CI: 23%, 53%) higher odds of being in the healthiest CHAI category.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Favorable early-life socioeconomic conditions support healthier aging among Chinese older adults, highlighting the need to address early-life inequalities to promote healthy aging.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Unraveling the Early-Life Influences on Healthy Aging: Insights From the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS)

                    <jats:p>Using longitudinal data, we investigate changes in coresidence preference of Chinese older adults and, with application of the Andersen-Newman framework, examine factors contributing to coresidence preference.</jats:p>

                    <jats:p>Data come from five waves of the Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey collected between 2005 and 2018. records.abstract: <jats:p>Timely diagnosis of dementia is critical, as early identification enables interventions that can meaningfully improve quality of life and support long-term planning for individuals and their families. Despite this, many Australians continue to receive a diagnosis at a late stage due to a range of personal, social, and structural barriers. BrainTrack, a freely available and evidence-based mobile application, was developed to help address this gap by supporting users to monitor their cognitive health and encouraging earlier engagement with healthcare professionals when concerns arise. This study sought to assess the broader social and economic value generated by BrainTrack. A Social Return on Investment (SROI) framework was employed to quantify the social outcomes associated with the app. Survey data collected 12 months after initial use captured five key outcomes: increased dementia literacy, enhanced dementia knowledge, reduced stigma, greater motivation to adopt cognitive health-promoting behaviours, and increased help-seeking intentions. Monetary values were assigned to each outcome to estimate the value created. Inputs included the resources invested in BrainTrack, such as initial development costs and ongoing maintenance. To determine the net impact, adjustments were made for deadweight, displacement, attribution, and drop-off prior to calculating the SROI ratio. Survey responses from 2,339 BrainTrack users informed the analysis. With an investment of AU$1.9 million over five years, the SROI analysis estimated a social return of approximately $5 for every $1 invested in BrainTrack. Sensitivity analyses showed ratios ranging from AU$0.86:1 to AU$24:1. The largest proportion of estimated social value was associated with increased motivation to change, whereas reduced stigma and increased help-seeking were associated with comparatively smaller estimated social value. Overall, BrainTrack was associated with social and economic value through cognitive self-monitoring, increased dementia awareness, and greater engagement with health services.</jats:p>
title: Social Return on Investment (SROI) of the BrainTrack App for Monitoring Brain Health Among Older Australians

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Osteoporosis (OP), a degenerative bone disease prevalent in aging populations, can lead to various complications and significantly impair the quality of life of elderly patients. We aimed to identify OP-related protein biomarkers and modifiable lifestyle factors for OP prevention in older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Summary-data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR) and colocalization analyses were conducted to assess the possible causal effects of plasma protein on OP. Genetic data for plasma proteins were derived from the deCODE (4907 proteins) and UK Biobank-PPP (2923 proteins) datasets. OP summary statistics were obtained from the FinnGen study (10,461 cases). Two-sample Mendelian randomization (TSMR) analyses were subsequently performed to evaluate the effects of lifestyle factors on OP-related proteins.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Primary SMR analysis identified 31 and 24 OP-related proteins in the deCODE and UKB-PPP cohorts, respectively. Cross-analysis of both datasets identified nine OP-related plasma protein targets. Among them, RSPO3 showed moderate evidence of colocalization with OP (PP.H4 = 0.643). TSMR analysis suggested that genetically predicted higher body mass index (BMI) was associated with increased RSPO3 levels (β = 0.08, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.14, p = 0.001), whereas type 2 diabetes (T2DM) was associated with lower RSPO3 levels (β = -5.71, 95% CI -11.16 to -0.26, p = 0.045).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study identified nine plasma protein biomarkers with genetic evidence supporting their association with OP risk, with RSPO3 showing the strongest supportive evidence among the prioritized targets. These findings offer new insights into OP etiology and highlight how metabolic traits may influence bone health via specific protein mediators.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Identification of Novel Protein Biomarkers and Lifestyle-Modifiable Targets for Osteoporosis: Evidence from Mendelian Randomization and Colocalization Analyses

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Physical performance measures are commonly used in geriatric assessment and have been associated with falls, but their ability to discriminate between older adults with and without falls may be limited. We compared the Timed Up and Go (TUG) test, gait speed, and grip strength within a population-based cohort, considering associations, discriminatory performance, incremental discrimination, and established clinical TUG thresholds.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We analyzed data from 1,079 community-dwelling adults aged ≥ 65 years participating in KORA-Age. Fall status was classified for 819 participants based on self-reported falls in the 12 months preceding the 3-year follow-up interview. Associations of baseline TUG, gait speed, and grip strength with reported falls were examined using sequential logistic regression models adjusted for age and sex, additional clinical covariates, and frailty. Discriminatory performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with DeLong tests used to evaluate incremental discrimination beyond age and sex. We additionally examined combinations of the three performance measures and predefined TUG thresholds. Inverse-probability weighting was used in sensitivity analyses to address selective follow-up.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Poorer TUG performance remained associated with reported falls after additional adjustment for frailty (OR per 1-s increase 1.095, 95% CI 1.018–1.176), whereas the association with slower gait speed was attenuated after frailty adjustment and grip strength was not associated with falls. The age- and sex-adjusted reference model had an AUC of 0.680; corresponding AUCs after adding TUG, gait speed, or grip strength were 0.700, 0.692, and 0.675, respectively, with no clear evidence of incremental discrimination. Combining all three performance measures did not improve discrimination beyond TUG alone. Higher TUG thresholds identified smaller groups with a higher prevalence of falls and greater specificity but progressively lower sensitivity. Inverse-probability-weighted analyses yielded similar associations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>TUG remained associated with reported falls after multivariable and additional frailty adjustment, but none of the three physical performance measures showed clear incremental discrimination beyond age and sex. Combining the measures did not improve discrimination, and established TUG thresholds showed limited sensitivity. These findings support distinguishing statistical associations with falls from the ability of physical performance measures to discriminate between older adults with and without falls.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Clinical trial number</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Not applicable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Aging is accompanied by progressive declines in cognitive and physical function. Dual-task training, which combines cognitive and motor demands, is a promising nonpharmacological approach, yet evidence that its benefits generalize beyond trained tasks and persist over time remains limited. This study examined the immediate and longer-term effects of a variable dual-task intervention on motor and cognitive function in community-dwelling older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Fifty adults aged ≥ 65 years, including participants meeting criteria for mild cognitive impairment, were randomly allocated to an intervention group (IG;
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 30) or waitlist control (WLC;
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 20). The IG completed a 12-week, twice-weekly program (24 sessions × 60 min) designed to be highly variable across cognitive and motor demands to minimize task-specific learning. Outcomes were assessed at baseline, post-intervention, and three-month follow-up, including the Timed Up and Go Test, Five Times Sit-to-Stand Test (5xSTS), Eriksen Flanker Test, Trail Making Test, and Digit Span Test. Between-group effects and long-term trajectories within the IG were analyzed using linear and generalized linear mixed models under an intention-to-treat approach.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The intervention produced a significant improvement in functional lower-limb strength relative to the WLC at post-intervention (5xSTS: Group × Time interaction
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.005, standardized mean difference [SMD] = 0.54), maintained within the IG at three-month follow-up. No significant between-group effects were observed for the remaining motor or cognitive outcomes at post-intervention. Within the IG, improvements in functional mobility (Timed Up and Go, SMD = 0.28), inhibitory control (Flanker reaction time, SMD = 0.40–0.42), and short-term memory (forward Digit Span, SMD = 0.62) were absent immediately post-intervention and emerged only at follow-up.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Variable dual-task training produced immediate gains in functional lower-limb strength that persisted at follow-up, alongside delayed improvements in functional mobility, inhibitory control, and short-term memory consistent with a post-training consolidation process. These findings suggest two complementary pathways: task-specific overlap between training and assessment may explain the immediate motor gains, whereas variable practice may foster broader cognitive and mobility benefits that emerge over time.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

                      ), retrospectively registered on 19/12/2025.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Hot weather is an established cardiovascular hazard, but patient-level evidence on how clinical vulnerability, cooling constraints and barriers to care interact in older cardiology outpatients remains limited.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a convergent mixed-methods study in the cardiology outpatient clinic of a tertiary university hospital in Zonguldak, Türkiye, from June to August 2026. A total of 680 consecutively recruited patients aged ≥ 65 years completed a structured interviewer-administered survey covering heat-related symptoms, housing and cooling capacity, health-care access and frailty assessed using the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS). The primary outcome was self-reported heat-related worsening of cardiovascular symptoms; secondary outcomes included care delay and marked impact on daily life. Multivariable logistic regression was used, and a pragmatic seven-domain heat-vulnerability index was explored. Twenty purposively sampled participants underwent semi-structured interviews, analysed thematically and integrated with the quantitative findings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Mean age was 71.3 ± 5.3 years and 48.1% were women. Inadequate effective cooling was reported by 82.4%, at least two heat-related symptoms by 75.9%, and heat-related care delay by 30.9%. Among participants giving a definite response, 52.1% reported symptom worsening, independently associated with heart failure (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.86, 95% CI 1.18–2.95), prolonged hot indoor exposure (aOR 1.82, 1.19–2.81), summer transport difficulty (aOR 1.65, 1.08–2.53) and greater frailty (aOR per CFS point 1.30, 1.09–1.55). Care delay was associated with limited or absent daytime support (aOR 2.99, 2.05–4.35), transport difficulty (aOR 2.59, 1.67–4.00), living alone (aOR 2.45, 1.62–3.70) and insufficient income (aOR 2.02, 1.34–3.03). Symptom worsening, care delay and daily-life impact increased across vulnerability categories. Interviews showed that effective cooling, access to care and social support depended on their practical usability rather than nominal availability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Heat-related burden in older cardiology outpatients extends beyond acute events to symptoms, daily functioning and continuity of care, consistent with a multidimensional pattern of clinical, environmental and social vulnerability. Frailty, effective cooling, transport and reliable support may be relevant domains for brief heat-health discussions in outpatient cardiovascular care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Clinical trial number</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Not applicable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Heat-related symptom worsening, cooling constraints, and care disruption among older cardiology outpatients: a convergent mixed-methods study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults with pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) are particularly vulnerable to multidimensional frailty. However, longitudinal evidence regarding patterns of frailty changes after antituberculosis treatment initiation and their associated factors remains limited. This study aimed to identify distinct trajectories of multidimensional frailty among older adults with pulmonary TB and to examine the associations of anxiety, depression, insomnia, and clinical characteristics with different frailty trajectories.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A prospective longitudinal study was conducted among 251 older adults with pulmonary TB. Multidimensional frailty was assessed using the Tilburg Frailty Indicator (TFI) at 1, 3, 9, and 12 months after initiation of antituberculosis treatment. At baseline, anxiety and depression were assessed using the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS), and insomnia was assessed using the Athens Insomnia Scale (AIS). Latent class growth analysis was used to identify distinct trajectories of multidimensional frailty. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression was subsequently applied to select candidate variables, followed by multinomial logistic regression to examine factors associated with trajectory membership.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Three distinct trajectories of multidimensional frailty were identified: high-frailty decreasing (13.1%), moderate-frailty improving (17.9%), and low-frailty persistent (68.9%) trajectory. Multinomial LASSO regression selected 14 candidate variables potentially associated with frailty trajectory membership. Compared with the low-frailty persistence trajectory, a history of smoking (OR = 4.668, 95% CI 1.217–7.904,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       = 0.025) was associated with greater odds of membership in the high-frailty decreasing trajectory. In contrast, higher albumin levels (OR = 0.892, 95% CI 0.798–0.996,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       = 0.043), absence of anxiety symptoms (OR = 0.093,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       = 0.001), absence of depressive symptoms (OR = 0.044,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001), and absence of insomnia (OR = 0.020,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001) were associated with lower odds of membership in the high-frailty decreasing trajectory. Compared with the low-frailty persistence trajectory, absence of anxiety symptoms, absence of insomnia, and absence of depressive symptoms were also associated with lower odds of membership in the moderate-frailty improvement trajectory.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Multidimensional frailty exhibited substantial heterogeneity among older adults with pulmonary TB during antituberculosis treatment. Baseline anxiety, depressive symptoms, and insomnia, together with albumin level, were associated with distinct frailty trajectories. Early frailty screening during antituberculosis treatment, integrated with assessment of psychological and sleep status and routine laboratory indicators, may facilitate trajectory-based risk stratification and individualized management of frailty in older adults with pulmonary TB.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Clinical trial number</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Not applicable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The oral health of nursing home residents is often poor. In the cluster-randomised controlled MundZaRR trial, a complex intervention to improve oral health was investigated across 18 nursing homes (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 271 participants). A comprehensive process evaluation aimed to explore the experiences of various target groups and gain insights into the implementation of the intervention.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The process evaluation followed international guidelines. The study was conducted in Germany and the data collection took place between July 2022 and October 2023 and comprised 23 individual, semi-structured interviews and three focus groups with dentists, dental assistants, nursing home managers and staff, and members of the resident council, 20 participatory observations, written surveys, structured protocols and document analysis. Quantitative data were analysed descriptively; qualitative data were analysed using content analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Three educational training courses over approximately nine hours for dentists and dental assistants were performed largely as planned and evaluated positively. The intervention could not be implemented in one out of nine nursing homes due to staff and time shortages, and the remaining intervention clusters showed considerable variations in implementation fidelity and cooperation between dental assistants and nursing home staff. Participatory observations revealed that individual oral care recommendations were only completely implemented in around half of the observed participants and that more specific oral care measures (e.g., interdental cleaning) were only rarely performed. The main barriers to the intervention’s implementation were staff and time shortages, lack of interest or engagement of nursing staff, and individual resident barriers (e.g., poor health condition, uncooperative behaviour). The COVID-19 pandemic posed a major challenge during the recruitment phase, but predominantly did not affect the further course of the study, according to the participating target groups.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Despite the overall positive perception of the intervention concept by the target groups, we found several inconsistencies in the implementation across the nursing homes of the intervention group. The barriers identified can provide indications for the future development and implementation of comparable oral health interventions in the nursing home setting.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Nutritional status and functional capacity are closely linked and contribute to healthy longevity. Given geographic isolation, Indigenous older adults are more likely to experience limited food diversity and suboptimal diets, increasing cardiometabolic risk in later life. Indigenous Taiwanese communities have distinct cultural identities, lifestyles, and food systems; therefore, health promotion programmes combining professional advice with culturally appropriate approaches are crucial.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This community-based participatory research (CBPR), titled ‘Engaging Native Abilities to Boost Lifestyle Enhancement’ (ENABLE), co-created nutrition and cooking workshops with the Indigenous Tsou community in Taiwan. Photovoice-facilitated focus groups were conducted with nine Indigenous older adults to explore dietary patterns before and after the workshops. Post-workshop interviews were conducted with 16 participants, including nine older adults and seven co-organisers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings reveal that health literacy is constructed and embodied in everyday practices through three interrelated processes shaped by health needs, social roles, and relational responsibility. First, ‘negotiating dietary decisions with health needs’ involves dialogue between traditional and scientific knowledge about food choice transitions. For example, some participants described transitioning from traditional roasted pork to fish in response to changes in chewing ability. Second, ‘engaging place-based adaptive strategies within lifestyles’ supports food access and maintenance of social roles. For example, work is central to Indigenous life, shaping identity, autonomy, and a sense of achievement; participants incorporated dietary portion control into their lifestyles to manage weight while maintaining strength for work. Third, ‘mobilising individual agency for collective well-being’ extends nutritional awareness to family and community members.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The CBPR approach, grounded in the lived experiences of Indigenous older adults, can shape a tailored dietary intervention. Meaningful engagement in Indigenous health research is strengthened by mutual understanding, shared action, and reflexive dialogue. Health literacy may support the agency of Indigenous older adults and local health sectors; however, its sustained effects in addressing structural barriers and supporting healthy ageing in place warrant further examination. Given the centrality of work in Indigenous life, health promotion activities may benefit from remaining flexible and collaborating with occupational groups to better connect working-aged adults, those transitioning into retirement, and older adults with increasing health needs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Health literacy in action through community-based participatory research: the ENABLE programme for indigenous older adults in Taiwan

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Musculoskeletal pain and psychosocial well-being both influence leisure-time physical activity (LTPA) in older adults, but their combined impact remains poorly understood. This study examines the impact of musculoskeletal pain and psychosocial well-being on LTPA trajectories in older adults and estimates the potential impact of improved energy levels on LTPA using simulation modeling.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In a community-based cohort of 2,209 older adults, we investigated whether baseline musculoskeletal and psychosocial well-being (perceived energy and social engagement) predicted 9-year LTPA trajectories. Two LTPA trajectory groups were identified: lower (45%, median[range]: 11[0–86] minutes walking/week) and higher (55%, median[range]: 111[10–1610] minutes walking/week). Logistic regression models examined associations of musculoskeletal pain, energy, and social engagement with LTPA trajectory group adjusting for demographics, health behaviors, and comorbidities. An interaction of psychosocial well-being by musculoskeletal pain was tested. A simulation analysis estimated how increasing energy among older adults with musculoskeletal pain could influence predicted LTPA group membership, and the number needed to treat (NNT) was calculated.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Baseline perceived energy, but not social engagement or musculoskeletal pain, consistently ranked among the top three predictors of LTPA across models. In adjusted logistic regression models, musculoskeletal pain was associated with a 40% lower likelihood of being in the higher LTPA trajectory; high energy corresponded with a 73% higher likelihood of being in the higher LTPA trajectory. Social engagement was associated with 33% higher LTPA, but only among men. The interaction between musculoskeletal pain and energy was not significant. After reassigning higher energy levels to older adults with low energy and musculoskeletal pain, the predicted probability of being in the higher LTPA trajectory increased from 41% to 50%, yielding an NNT of 11.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Perceived energy is a strong, independent predictor of LTPA, even in the presence of musculoskeletal pain. Simulated increase in energy among 11 older adults with pain corresponded with one additional person in the higher LTPA trajectory, an effect comparable to current behavioral interventions. Supporting psychosocial wellbeing may offer a valuable approach to promoting LTPA in older adults alongside pain management.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cognitive training may enhance cognition and support brain health during aging, but few trials have evaluated readily accessible chatbot-based programs with neuroimaging outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to evaluate the effects of a chatbot-based cognitive training program on white matter microstructural organization and cognition in cognitively unimpaired older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In a single-blind randomized controlled trial, 72 cognitively unimpaired older adults were assigned to chatbot-based cognitive training (30 min/day, 5 days/week for 12 weeks; n=37) or a no-intervention control (n=35). Diffusion tensor imaging at baseline and 12 weeks quantified fractional anisotropy (FA) in predefined white matter tracts, and cognition was assessed with the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Groups were comparable at baseline. After 12 weeks, the training group showed significantly less FA reduction than controls in the bilateral tapetum and right posterior thalamic radiation, surviving false discovery rate control (P<.05). The training group also improved on Paired Associates Learning (PAL), an episodic memory measure (P=.04). PAL improvement was positively associated with FA change in the right posterior thalamic radiation and right sagittal stratum (false discovery rate–adjusted P=.04 for each).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings suggest that a 12-week chatbot-based cognitive training program may support episodic memory and the relative maintenance of white matter microstructural organization in selected pathways in cognitively unimpaired older adults, consistent with a brain-maintenance framework.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Technology-based rehabilitation is increasingly used for balance training in older adults. A 2023 network meta-analysis (NMA) found only exergaming with motion capture superior to no treatment; however, the evidence has since expanded, and no GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) appraisal has been applied.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to update the comparative effectiveness of 5 technology categories—exergaming with balance platforms (EBP), exergaming with motion capture (EMC), other serious games, interventions with wearables, and telerehabilitation (Tele)—versus conventional exercise (CE), and no treatment (NT), applying GRADE adapted for NMA.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A systematic search of 4 databases from inception through April 2025, with an identical supplementary update search to January 31, 2026, identified 60 randomized controlled trials (N=3469; mean age 73.1, SD 5.2; range 63.3-86.2 y). Fifty-seven trials (2758 analyzed participants) contributed to 4 prespecified networks (all balance, functional scales, Timed Up and Go [TUG] test, and gait speed). A random-effects NMA was fitted using multivariate meta-regression. Treatment hierarchies were summarized by the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) and the probability of being best; certainty of evidence was rated with GRADE adapted for NMA.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      In the all-balance network, Tele (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.69, 95% CI 0.08‐1.29;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.03), EBP (SMD 0.63, 95% CI 0.31‐0.95;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001), EMC (SMD 0.58, 95% CI 0.22‐0.95;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.002), and CE (SMD 0.35, 95% CI 0.03‐0.68;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.03) were superior to NT, with consistent findings in the TUG network (EBP 0.81, 95% CI 0.42‐1.20; Tele 0.82, 95% CI 0.16‐1.49; EMC 0.79, 95% CI 0.36‐1.21; all
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.05). Tele ranked first by SUCRA (76.3%), but its probability of being best was only approximately 41%, and the estimate rested on 5 trials (n=198). No technology-based intervention was superior to CE in any network. Certainty of evidence was moderate for EBP versus NT and EMC versus NT in the TUG network only; the 37 other comparisons were low or very low. Dropout did not differ between technology-based and control arms (odds ratio 1.10, 95% CI 0.87‐1.40;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.41).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Tele, EBP, and EMC were each associated with improved balance versus NT, although none exceeded CE. The first-place SUCRA ranking of Tele is preliminary. Certainty was moderate only for EBP and EMC versus NT on the TUG test; the remaining evidence is too uncertain for firm clinical recommendations. As no included trial reported falls, these findings are not direct evidence of fall prevention. Larger trials with standardized comparator intensity and posttraining follow-up are required.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Comparative Effectiveness of Digital Exercise-Based Interventions for Improving Balance in Older Adults: Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis With GRADE Certainty of Evidence

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Delirium is common among older adults, particularly those with cognitive impairment. However, delirium among patients with dementia or mild cognitive impairment (MCI) in long-term care (LTC) hospitals has received limited attention.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to examine delirium occurrence and associated factors among patients with dementia or MCI in LTC hospitals.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This cross-sectional study included 142 patients aged 65 years or older with dementia (n=100, 70.4%) or MCI (n=42, 29.6%) at 2 LTC hospitals in South Korea between September 2021 and August 2022. Delirium occurrence was defined as at least 1 positive Short Confusion Assessment Method assessment during twice-daily assessments over 4 weeks, including the first assessment. Multivariable logistic regression examined associated factors overall and within each cognitive group.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Delirium was identified in 55 (38.7%) of 142 patients. The proportion was 41% (41/100) in patients with dementia and 33.3% (14/42) in patients with MCI. Hypoactive delirium was the most common subtype (33/55, 60%). Overall, female sex (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 4.344, 95% CI 1.794-10.515; P=.001), immobility (aOR 4.953, 95% CI 1.857-13.205; P=.001), and analgesic use (aOR 3.641, 95% CI 1.262-10.501; P=.02) were associated with delirium. Infection was inversely associated with delirium (aOR 0.251, 95% CI 0.101-0.623; P=.003). In patients with dementia, female sex, immobility, analgesic use, and pain were associated with delirium. Diaper use was associated with delirium in patients with MCI.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Delirium was common among patients with dementia or MCI in LTC hospitals. The findings support regular delirium assessment, with attention to mobility and pain-related care needs. Further studies are needed to clarify the factors associated with delirium in each cognitive group.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Delirium Occurrence and Associated Factors Among Patients With Dementia and Mild Cognitive Impairment Admitted to Long-Term Care Hospitals: Cross-Sectional Study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>High-resolution digital cognitive tools administered at frequent intervals enable the study of age-related cognitive change at a previously unattainable level of granularity. Computational modeling further enables the simultaneous examination of multiple aspects of cognitive performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The objective of this study was to examine whether repeated digital multiday learning assessments can detect age-related cognitive decline over short time frames in cognitively unimpaired older adults and to quantify age-related differences in process-based cognitive markers derived from computational modeling.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 209 cognitively unimpaired older adults (mean age 73.6, SD 8.2 years; n=136, 65.1% female) from the Harvard Aging Brain Study and affiliated studies were administered the Boston Remote Assessment for Neurocognitive Health, which includes the face-name task, a paired associative learning task. Daily median response times for correct responses were used as the primary outcome. A new version of the face-name task was administered across up to 4 testing intervals over a mean of 2.8 (SD 0.4) years. Using computational modeling, we estimated longitudinal changes in peak performance, a practice-adjusted marker of an individual’s best expected response time, as an indicator of age-related cognitive decline. We further examined age-related differences in peak performance, stability (within-person variability), learning within and across testing intervals, and between-interval forgetting, with embedded linear regressions for age, sex, years of education, and device type.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Peak performance slowed by 0.04 seconds per year (95% credible interval 0.02-0.06; approximately 2% per year), indicating age-related cognitive decline. Higher age (+1-SD) was associated with slower peak performance (+0.19 seconds, 95% credible interval 0.12-0.26), steeper annual slowing in peak performance (+0.036 seconds per year), greater within-person variability (+0.043 seconds), reduced learning across testing intervals, and more forgetting.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our findings indicate that a digital multiday learning paradigm combined with computational modeling of response times sensitively detects age-related cognitive decline over short timescales (<3 years), which are difficult to capture in conventional study designs relying on infrequent assessments. In addition, this approach identifies specific process-based cognitive markers associated with aging, including slower performance, reduced stability, and diminished learning across testing intervals.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Detection of Age-Related Cognitive Decline Over Short Time Frames Using Digital Multiday Learning Assessments: Longitudinal Study

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Telemonitoring offers solutions for remote health management among older adults; yet, acceptance varies based on individual perceptions and presentation strategies.</jats:p>

                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This 2-phased sequential mixed methods study examines the role of message framing on telemonitoring adoption among low-income older adults.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Phase 1 involved in-depth interviews with 17 older adults, identifying key facilitators (accessibility, affordability, and health benefits) and barriers (preference for in-person consultations, technological limitations, and information processing difficulties) of telemonitoring. Building on these insights, phase 2 used an experimental study with 120 participants assessing message framing effects (episodic vs thematic) and modalities (video vs photo-text) on telemonitoring adoption.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Episodic framing did not produce a significant main effect on attitudes toward telemonitoring; however, its effect was moderated by external locus of control (LOC), with episodic framing associated with more positive attitudes among participants lower in external LOC, and thematic framing more favorable among those higher in external LOC.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Convenience, cost, and health benefits emerged as key adoption drivers, while traditional consultation preferences and cognitive processing challenges posed barriers. Theoretical and practical implications were discussed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Close relationships that are characterized by both positive and negative qualities (i.e., ambivalent ties) are common in later life and often give rise to interpersonal tensions with deleterious consequences for well-being. However, little is known about their effect on cognitive health. These effects may depend on seldom-studied interpersonal coping strategies that may either stimulate or deplete cognitive resources. This study tested whether ambivalent ties relate to lower cognitive functioning among older adults, and whether interpersonal coping strategies moderate these associations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As part of the Daily Experiences and Well-being Study (DEWS), participants (N = 271, ages 65-89) completed an in-person baseline interview assessing positive and negative qualities of their close social relationships and overall cognitive functioning (composite of four tests), followed by a self-administered questionnaire assessing three interpersonal coping strategies (engaged, avoidant, destructive).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Linear regression models revealed that a greater proportion of ambivalent ties was associated with worse overall cognitive functioning, but this association was not moderated by any interpersonal coping strategy. Sensitivity analyses of the separate cognitive tests revealed, unexpectedly, that greater use of engaged coping strengthened the association between ambivalent ties and worse executive functioning performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A greater proportion of ambivalent ties in one’s social network is associated with lower cognitive functioning among older adults, a link that may not easily be buffered through coping. Results suggest that ambivalent ties are an understudied important potential risk factor for adverse cognitive outcomes in later life.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Ambivalent close ties and cognitive functioning: Does coping play a role?

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Adult foster care may represent a viable alternative to nursing homes for dependent older adults. This study aimed to estimate the annual and daily cost of adult foster care for older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The Karukera Study of Aging in Foster Families is a prospective, one-year observational study including adults aged 60+ living in adult foster care in the French Caribbean Islands. We measured healthcare resource utilization using the RUD (Resource Utilization in Dementia)-Lite instrument. Costs related to healthcare consumption, foster caregiver remuneration, and training were estimated and expressed per patient-year.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 106 older adults (mean age: 82.2±11.2 years; 61.3% women) were followed for one year (mean follow-up duration: 306.1±90.8 days). The daily cost of outpatient care was estimated at €33.3, of which €29.9 corresponded to community nursing visits.                     <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Compared with a daily cost of €121 per resident in metropolitan nursing homes and €150 per resident in nursing homes in the French Caribbean Islands, adult foster care reduced costs by 20.6% and 35.9%, respectively. <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Healthy aging among older adults with cognitive impairment requires preserving physical, cognitive, and psychosocial functioning to sustain their independence and quality of life. However, existing interventions vary in design, delivery format, and composition, and evidence regarding their effectiveness across these three core domains remains inconsistent. This study aimed to identify the most effective intervention types for specific domains of healthy aging.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Five electronic databases were searched for studies published from October 2015 to June 2026. Randomized controlled trials reporting at least two outcomes—among physical capability, cognitive function, or psychosocial well-being—were reviewed. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk-of-Bias 2 tool. A dependency-aware multilevel random-effects meta-analysis with trial-clustered robust inference was conducted in R, supplemented by moderator tests, prediction intervals, sensitivity analyses, reporting-bias assessments, and GRADE evaluations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Multicomponent interventions were associated with beneficial effects on cognitive and psychosocial outcomes, whereas group-based interventions showed beneficial effects across all three domains and a significantly greater effect on cognitive function than individually delivered interventions. Despite substantial heterogeneity and wide prediction intervals, these findings were generally robust across sensitivity analyses.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The observed advantages of group-based delivery, particularly for cognitive function, and multicomponent approaches for cognitive and psychosocial outcomes highlight the domain-specific nature of intervention effects. These findings support tailoring intervention delivery and component configuration to the targeted domain rather than applying a uniform approach to healthy aging among older adults with cognitive impairment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Intervention-Type-Specific Effects on Healthy Aging of Older Adults with Cognitive Impairment: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
