<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Extreme climate events can threaten older adults’ health. The purpose of this study was to summarize existing literature on older adults’ climate health literacy, defined as their ability to find and access, understand, and act upon information related to climate-related health threats.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A scoping review was conducted in the bibliographic databases Embase, Medline and Scopus and grey literature sources Cornell Initiative for Research on Climate and Aging and Climate Change and Human Health Literature portals with searches updated January 2026. English language studies of community-dwelling adults aged 60 years and older were included if they reported at least one aspect of climate health literacy. Quantitative data were reported as median percentages, and qualitative themes were categorized.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Fifty-nine studies, including 22,992 records for 20,296 unique participants, were included. Most recognized the health risks of extreme climate events but did not identify personal vulnerability. Television was the most cited source of information and hydration, clothing and environment modification, and activity adjustment were the most utilized adaptive actions. Barriers to adaptive actions included financial constraints, limited mobility and lack of supports. The effectiveness of studied interventions was mixed, influenced by intervention type and study design.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Despite access to information and awareness of climate-related health threats, gaps remain in personal risk perception and translation of knowledge into actions. Improving climate health literacy among older adults requires public health messaging, engagement of trustworthy authorities, and interventions addressing social and structural barriers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Perceptions, Knowledge, and Adaptive actions in Response to Climate Events: A Scoping Review of Climate Health Literacy among Community Dwelling Older Adults

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The global aging population has led to an increasing number of older active drivers. While age-related physical and cognitive changes are associated with increased crash risk, specific on-road adaptations and safety outcomes of older drivers remain unclear. This study examined distinct driving characteristics, personality traits, and cognitive processes related to decision-making among middle-aged and older drivers in a simulated driving environment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We assessed driving performance in a high-fidelity motorcycle simulator across drivers in three age groups: middle-aged (30-54; n = 40), aged 65–74 (n = 34), and aged 75 + (75-86; n = 29). Comparative analysis focused on speed regulation, braking behavior, control stability, and accident rates. Additionally, questionnaire measures and a computerized decision-making task were employed to assess risk perception and risky decision-making.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Compared to the middle-aged group, both older groups demonstrated a significantly more conservative driving profile: lower mean speeds, fewer speeding violations, longer braking maneuvers, reduced variation in throttle control, and a lower incidence of simulated accidents. Drivers aged 75+ also reported higher perceived risk in driving scenarios and displayed diminished discrimination between risk and non-risk situations in a braking decision task. Mediation analyses showed that steering variance in the simulator and self-reported health/safety risk-taking significantly mediated the relationship between age group and number of accidents.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings indicate that older drivers adopt proactive compensatory strategies that could result in fewer simulated accidents. These findings challenge a purely deficit-oriented perspective on older driver safety, underscoring the critical role of behavioral adaptation and strategic self-regulation in maintaining safe mobility.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Adaptive driving, not unsafe: Older drivers’ compensatory strategies and lower simulated crash risk

                    <jats:p>Neighborhood satisfaction is a key indicator of well-being and community quality of life, yet its relationship with third place engagement remains underexplored.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines how third place engagement, access, and perceived built environments relate to physical livability, social connectedness, and overall neighborhood satisfaction among older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Survey data were collected from 515 adults aged 65 and older in the Orlando area, and separate Ordinary Least Squares regression models were used.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results indicate that neighborhood satisfaction is multidimensional, with shared yet distinct correlates across domains. Third place engagement and walkable access were consistently associated with all three outcomes. Socially oriented third place use was more closely tied to social connectedness, while built environment quality aligned with physical livability. Overall satisfaction reflected both domains, highlighting the value of viewing neighborhood satisfaction as related but distinct constructs shaped by functional and social experiences among older adults.</jats:p>

records.abstract: <jats:p>Background: Family co-residence is often considered protective for older adults in India but may not ensure inclusion in household decisions. This study examined how widowhood and decision-making exclusion are jointly associated with depressive symptoms among co-resident older adults. Methods: Data came from LASI Wave 1 (2017–18) and included 27,840 married or widowed adults aged 60+. Survey-weighted logistic regression examined widowhood, decision-making exclusion, their interaction, dose-response patterns, and sex-stratified associations with CES-D depressive symptoms. Results: Decision-making exclusion was highest among widowed women and lowest among married men. More extensive exclusion was associated with higher depressive symptoms, while widowhood without exclusion was not significant after full adjustment. There was little evidence that widowhood and exclusion interacted. Associations with depressive symptoms were more clearly observed among women than men. Conclusion: Among co-resident older adults, having a meaningful voice in family decisions may be important for mental health beyond shared residence alone.</jats:p>
title: Family Decision-Making Exclusion, Widowhood, and Depressive Symptoms Among Co-Resident Older Adults in India

records.abstract: <jats:p>We examine racial disparities in the association between work discrimination and life satisfaction among older adults and whether any differences are mediated by one’s sense of personal mastery using data from the 2010 and 2012 waves of the Health and Retirement Study. The results from the structural equation models (SEM) show White people who experience work discrimination report the lowest life satisfaction, followed by Hispanic and then Black people. After accounting for the mediating effect of one’s sense of mastery to cope with discriminatory work experiences, we find work discrimination still has a direct negative association with the life satisfaction of White and Black respondents but the effect for Hispanic people is no longer statistically significant. The results of the direct and total effects also suggest the mediating effects of mastery on the association between work discrimination and life satisfaction among older workers is strongest for White people, followed by Hispanic people and then Black people. These findings suggest that a person’s efficiency at drawing upon their coping resources like mastery when needed is essential for protecting their well-being from the harmful effects of work discrimination, especially for Black and Hispanic people.</jats:p>
title: Mastery as a Mediator for the Effects of Work Discrimination on Racial Disparities in Life Satisfaction

records.abstract: <jats:p>This study examined discrepancies between persons living with dementia (PLWD) and their spousal caregivers in the perceived importance of PLWD’s care needs, and how caregivers’ dementia knowledge and empathy were associated with these discrepancies. Data were drawn from 65 couples managing early-stage Alzheimer’s disease. PLWD self-reported the importance of their physical, psychological, and social needs, while caregivers provided proxy ratings. PLWD perceived addressing their physical needs as more important than did their caregivers, whereas both partners agreed on the importance of psychological and social needs. Caregivers’ greater empathic concern was associated with smaller discrepancies in the perceived importance of physical needs; greater personal distress was associated with smaller discrepancies in social needs. Caregivers’ dementia knowledge was positively associated with discrepancies in psychological needs only when relationship quality was lower. These findings highlight the importance of caregivers’ emotional responsiveness and relational dynamics in caregiver interventions, expanding the focus beyond dementia knowledge.</jats:p>
title: Spousal Discrepancy in Perceived Importance of Care Needs Among Couples Managing Early-Stage Alzheimer’s Disease

records.abstract: <jats:p>We examined associations between sexual activity, sexual quality, and glycosylated hemoglobin (HbA1c) levels among partnered older adults with diabetes. Using longitudinal data from the National Social Life, Health, and Aging Project, we studied 620 partnered respondents with diabetes aged 57 to 85 at baseline. We estimated mixed-effects models of sexual activity, frequency, and quality on HbA1c trajectories over ten years, including tests for gender differences. Results indicated that being sexually active and having sex a few times a month were associated with more favorable HbA1c trajectories compared to being sexually inactive. Emotional satisfaction was associated with worsening HbA1c trajectories for women but stable trajectories for men. Physical pleasure showed no gender differences. The findings suggest that partnered sexuality is a meaningful, gendered aspect of older adults’ metabolic health that deserves greater attention as a dimension of diabetes care in later life.</jats:p>
title: Sexuality and Glycosylated Hemoglobin Levels in Partnered Older Adults With Diabetes

records.abstract: <jats:p>This study investigates how retirement’s effect on subsequent health varies by individual attributes and their interaction. Instead of spotlighting heterogeneity for a specific, theoretically predetermined feature, I consider the feature-wide effect heterogeneity to find possible data-driven candidates that generate this heterogeneity. To accomplish this, I use causal forests and harmonized data from the Gateway to Global Aging Data (the Gateway). The results show that temporal dimensions (such as age and birth cohort) and financial dimensions (such as income and wealth) are the most important features in heterogenizing retirement’s effect on health. Based on these findings, I suggest the “double scaffold” model to comprehensively explain feature-wide effect heterogeneity.</jats:p>
title: Double Scaffold of Retirement on Subsequent Health: Revisiting Spatio-Temporality and Finance Through the Feature-Wide Effect Heterogeneity

records.abstract: <jats:p>More than 60% of older workers report experiencing ageism in the workplace, yet little is known about whether the relationship between ageism, job satisfaction, and mental health differs by US-born status. This study examined whether job satisfaction mediates the association between workplace ageism and depressive symptoms and assessed whether this association differs by US-born status. Data were drawn from the 2018 and 2020 National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1979 for workers aged 53- 62, and a multiple-group path analysis was conducted. The results indicated that, among US-born workers, job satisfaction significantly mediated the associations between depressive symptoms and both ageism in promotion and ageism in early retirement. Among immigrant workers, however, this mediating effect was significant only for ageism in promotion. Findings underscore the importance of developing anti-ageism policies that adopt an intersectional approach, jointly considering US-born status and age to reduce the detrimental impacts of ageism on workers’ mental health.</jats:p>
title: Workplace Ageism, Job Satisfaction, and Depressive Symptoms Among Older Workers: The Roles of US-Born Status

records.abstract: <jats:p>As populations age and the share of retirees increases across Europe, the question of whether individuals stay active after retirement is increasingly salient. Retirees are known to provide more instrumental support than their working counterparts. However, most previous studies have relied on between-group comparisons of retirees and employed individuals, leaving it unclear how the transition into retirement affects changes in instrumental support within individuals over time. Using eight waves of the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe covering 19 countries between 2004–2022 (n = 7,422 observations from 3,711 individuals aged 50+), we employed fixed-effects regression and found that the transition from employment to retirement was associated with an increase in instrumental support provision outside the household. We also found suggestive evidence that this association was stronger in countries with higher social expenditures. These findings indicate that retirement may promote activity and facilitate engagement in helping others.</jats:p>
title: Changes in Instrumental Support Around Retirement: Longitudinal Evidence From Europe

records.abstract: <jats:p>Older adults who need community services may remain uncertain whether those services are locally provided or judge that they are not. Research on perceived unmet need often combines these positions. Using a cross-sectional survey of 929 adults aged 60 or older in urban Jiangsu, China, we paired reported need with perceived provision across 20 services and distinguished awareness gaps, perceived non-provision, and comparison uncertainty for services not reported as needed. Fractional logit models examined associations with social participation and functional status. Greater social participation was associated with fewer awareness gaps, concentrated among adults with ADL disability (−8.75 percentage points per SD). A weaker, less stable association with perceived non-provision appeared among functionally independent adults, and no counterpart appeared for comparison uncertainty. Unresolved uncertainty and negative provision judgments may call for different responses, and outreach may be especially relevant for older adults with ADL disability.</jats:p>
title: Need-Conditioned Uncertainty and Perceived Non-Provision of Community Services: Social Participation and Functional Status Among Older Adults in Urban China

records.abstract: <jats:p>Psychotherapeutic interventions can support people with dementia. Family members often play a pivotal role in the therapeutic process but little is known about their experiences of therapy, how they perceive the impact on their relative, and how the experience affects them directly. This study aimed to explore the experiences of family members who engage in therapy, or support someone living with dementia to attend therapy. Individuals with dementia and their family members were recruited as participants through NHS Trusts, professional networks, social media and community and support groups based in England and Wales. Semi-structured qualitative individual or dyadic interviews were conducted with 17 participants, eight of whom were living with dementia and nine were family members. Framework analysis was used. Family members highlighted “the importance of feeling seen” as distinct individuals by clinicians when engaging with psychotherapy, and not just the carer of their partner. When working with “dementia as dynamic phenomenon”, therapeutic approaches needed to balance being sufficiently structured and containing whilst allowing for adaptions to each individual changeable presentation. Participants highlighted how psychotherapy presented “expected and unexpected outcomes”, challenges that arose when outcomes were not agreed upon, and how therapy functioned as a support structure in ways the participants did not foresee. Psychotherapeutic intervention provides meaningful support to the family members of individuals with dementia. Understanding the needs of family members, alongside the needs of the individual with dementia, and taking a systemic approach is conducive to better therapeutic outcomes. The changeable nature of dementia presentation means that a therapeutic approach should be flexible based on the needs of the family. Psychotherapeutic intervention with individuals with dementia can have a range of benefits for the individual and the wider family, when sufficient considerations are made to understand each person’s needs.</jats:p>
title: The Experiences of Psychotherapy for People With Dementia: A Qualitative Interview Study With Family Members

records.abstract: <jats:p>Person-centered care (PCC) is the gold standard for improving the quality of life (QoL) of people living with dementia. The Montessori method represents a practical model for implementing PCC in Nursing Homes (NHs). To date, no study has documented how residents describe their QoL in NHs implementing this method using a self-report approach consistent with PCC principles. This study explores residents’ perceptions of their QoL, as well as how they relate it to the care model, using a qualitative self-assessment tool. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with twenty-nine residents from two NHs with high levels of Montessori implementation assessed using a validated tool. All interviews were analyzed using thematic analysis. Three interconnected themes emerged. The first examines the components of QoL that matter most to residents. The second explores how the care model influences these determinants. Finally, the third describes residents’ self-assessment of QoL shaped by individual factors. Our study contributes to a better understanding of the Montessori method as a comprehensive PCC model from residents’ perspectives and deepens knowledge of the extent to which it can shape their QoL. These findings also provide practical and methodological insights for evaluating QoL and guiding care models promoting QoL.</jats:p>
title: Exploring Quality of Life Through Residents’ Voice in Nursing Homes: A Qualitative Study of a Montessori-Based Person-Centered Model of Care

records.abstract: <jats:p>Purpose: People with dementia can and do live successfully on their own, but there are additional challenges for people living alone without informal support. This paper reports findings of the first study in the UK to examine needs and experiences of, and services for, people with dementia who live alone without informal support. Method: The study involved a service audit of 13 local authority commissioners in two English regions, interviews with 22 people with dementia who live alone without informal carers, and case studies of four services supporting this group. Findings: Awareness of this population among commissioners was limited. There were very few services which explicitly supported this group, and some mainstream services excluded people without carers. None of the local authorities collected data on numbers of people with dementia living alone, or those without informal support, in their area. Some participants with dementia had contacted social care, but this had not always resulted in appropriate support, and people reported problematic interactions with staff, assumptions that friends would provide care, and support not being available at the right time. Self-funders were left with little support. People with dementia were resourceful, using general services, technology, and other tactics, including cleaners, meal delivery, community taxis, and automatic reminders to organise their lives. However, as many of these additional services have a cost attached, there is potential to exacerbate existing inequalities. Participants wanted more support, particularly with finances and administrative tasks. Services can help this group with supported handovers, allowing self-referral back into a service, and keeping case files open. Conclusions: Both the number of people with dementia, and the number of people ageing without children, are rising, and it will therefore become increasingly important to facilitate effective support for people with dementia to live independently without informal support.</jats:p>
title: Living Alone With Dementia: Managing Without Informal Support to Contact and Navigate Services

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Motor dysfunction is associated with cognitive vulnerability, but whether impairments across body regions jointly contribute to motoric cognitive risk syndrome (MCR) remains unclear. We examined the independent and joint associations of handgrip strength and chair-stand test (CST) with MCR.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This cross-sectional study included 6258 dementia-free older adults (mean age 71.5 ± 6.6 years; 63.1% women) from a community-based cohort. Handgrip strength and CST performance were used to define upper- and lower-extremity motor impairment. Participants were classified as normal, handgrip weakness only, CST impairment only, or combined motor impairment. Multivariable logistic regression was performed with adjustment for demographic, socioeconomic, lifestyle, and clinical factors. Additive and multiplicative interactions were assessed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>MCR was present in 10.4% of participants. Using the A/B CST cutoff as the primary definition, adjusted odds ratios (95% confidence intervals) for MCR, compared with normal function, were 1.84 (1.14–2.97) for handgrip weakness only, 4.17 (2.97–5.85) for CST impairment only, and 9.17 (6.56–12.81) for combined motor impairment. Associations were directionally consistent across alternative CST cutoffs. A positive additive interaction was observed at the A/B CST cutoff (relative excess risk due to interaction = 3.48; attributable proportion = 0.40; and synergy index = 1.83), whereas multiplicative interaction was not positive.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Combined handgrip weakness and poorer CST performance were strongly associated with prevalent MCR. A positive additive interaction at the primary CST cutoff suggests that joint motor impairment may help characterize MCR-related vulnerability in older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Joint associations of handgrip strength and chair-stand performance with motoric cognitive risk syndrome in older adults

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) is the most common cause of hospitalization in older adults. Cellular senescence, a hallmark of aging biology, has been implicated in heart failure pathophysiology and functional decline via the pro-inflammatory senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). We evaluated the association between SASP and physical function in older adults hospitalized for ADHF.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>REHAB-HF was a trial of older adults hospitalized for ADHF randomized to a novel physical rehabilitation intervention or attention control. We measured a panel of 18-SASP analytes at in-hospital baseline and at 3-month follow-up. Outcomes included short physical performance battery (SPPB) and 6-minute walk distance (6MWD). Statistical analysis included principal component analysis (PCA) of log- and z-transformed SASP values. Associations were evaluated with multivariable regression models adjusted for age, sex, and intervention arm.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Samples were available for 226 (65%) of the REHAB-HF participants with mean age (SD) 72.3 (8), 53% female, 52% HFpEF, and 53% assigned to rehab intervention. Principal Component 1 (PC1) reflected a coordinated signal across biomarkers of inflammation and immune signaling. PC1 was associated with poorer function at baseline [(SPPB -0.46 [-0.77, -0.14]; p = 0.004 and 6MWD -19.7 meters [-32.7, -6.7]; p = 0.003)]. Increasing SASP over time was associated with clinically significant reduced physical function improvement (ΔSPPB -1.80 [-2.58, -1.03]; p &lt; 0.001 and Δ6MWD -49.7 meters [-77.2, -22.1]; p = 0.001).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Higher SASP levels were associated with poorer physical function recovery in older patients hospitalized for ADHF. These findings suggest that inflammatory SASP biomarkers may improve risk stratification and potentially guide therapeutic strategies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>REHAB-HF trial is registered at clinicaltrials.gov Clinical Trial Registry</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>NCT02196038</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Senescence Biomarkers Predict Physical Function and Clinical Outcomes After Heart Failure Hospitalization: Insights From REHAB-HF

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Polypharmacy is common in people living with dementia (PLwD) and associated with adverse outcomes. Although Structured Medication Reviews (SMRs) are recommended to optimise medication regimens, their delivery is often constrained by limited resources. Artificial intelligence (AI) may support SMRs, yet little is known about how it is perceived by PLwD and their carers. This study explored their experiences of polypharmacy, views on SMRs and attitudes towards use of AI tools in SMRs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Semi-structured interviews with 12 PLwD experiencing polypharmacy and two focus groups with 14 carers were conducted via Microsoft Teams or telephone and analysed using Reflexive Thematic Analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Two themes were constructed: participants’ perspectives on meaningful SMRs, and embracing AI while preserving patient safety and the human touch. Participants described challenges in managing polypharmacy, with carers playing a central role in supporting adherence and monitoring side effects. Experiences of SMRs varied. SMRs were most valued when clinicians were empathetic and able to offer personalised guidance. Participants viewed AI use in SMRs positively, provided that such tools were well validated and used to assist rather than replace healthcare professionals. AI was also seen as potentially reducing administrative burden and supporting more person-centred care. However, some had concerns regarding patient safety and data security, highlighting the need for appropriate regulation and human oversight.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participants were supportive of AI use in SMRs, despite concerns about safety, data security and disclosure of AI use, and emphasised the importance of patient-clinician interactions and lived experience involvement in AI tool development.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Attitudes of people living with dementia and their carers towards the use of generative artificial intelligence to inform structured medication reviews

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Bedridden older people generally have poor comprehensive capacity and are prone to multi-system complications including pressure injuries and lower limb venous thrombosis, imposing heavy caregiving and financial burdens and severely affecting their health.</jats:p>

                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Participants</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Two hundred twenty six bedridden older people aged 65 years and above from two nursing homes in China.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Patients were required 5 assessments during 1-year follow-up period. Latent Growth Mixture Modelling identified distinct trajectories, multinomial logistic regression identified characteristics distinguishing the trajectories and generalised estimating equations evaluated associations between trajectories and pressure injury and DVT.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>There are three distinct trajectories of comprehensive capacity among bedridden older people, including severe impairment with stable type (63.5%); moderate impairment with slowly deteriorating type (16.3%); moderate-to-severe impairment with fluctuating type (20.2%). Characteristics distinguishing the trajectories were tooth loss, hypertension, indwelling gastric tube and dysphagia. Compared with the severe impairment stable type, the other two groups had higher pressure injury risk; the moderate impairment with slowly deteriorating type also had higher DVT risk.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Capacity trajectories of bedridden older people are heterogeneous. Nurses may want to focus on those with tooth loss, hypertension, indwelling gastric tube and dysphagia to deliver targeted care. These trajectories are significantly associated with pressure injury and deep vein thrombosis risks. Their identification enables earlier risk stratification and more targeted prevention.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The trajectories of comprehensive capacity of bedridden older people based on latent growth mixture models: a longitudinal study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Extreme heat is a major environmental threat to healthy ageing, with older people experiencing the highest rates of heat-related morbidity and mortality. Although age-related physiological changes, multimorbidity and frailty remain key determinants of heat susceptibility, climate change, social inequalities and energy insecurity are reshaping the conditions in which older people experience and respond to thermal stress. This narrative New Horizons review integrates evidence identified through a structured, non-systematic search of peer-reviewed literature and relevant institutional reports across geriatric medicine, environmental health and climate science. It examines how frailty, intrinsic capacity, housing, energy affordability and social frailty influence the ability of older people to recognise risk, access protection and respond effectively to extreme heat. Particular attention is given to energy insecurity and summer cooling poverty, through which limited access to affordable household energy may undermine resilience. Ageing models primarily characterise individual vulnerability and functioning within the environment, whereas climate vulnerability models organise risk around exposure, sensitivity and adaptation; we use adaptive capacity to connect these perspectives by asking whether personal and contextual resources can be mobilised for protection. It may provide a conceptual basis for developing and subsequently validating a heat-adapted comprehensive geriatric assessment and for informing targeted prevention and climate adaptation policies for ageing populations.</jats:p>
title: New horizons in adaptive capacity and heat-related health in older people: integrating frailty, energy insecurity and social resources

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) serves as a model to study muscle plasticity and recovery. Exercise recovery declines with age, and while omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (n-3 PUFA) exhibit inconsistent effects in younger adults, the effect in older adults is unknown.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial, 43 healthy, older women and men (65-85 years) ingested 5 mL of n-3 PUFA algae oil (2 g PUFA) or placebo for eight weeks. After eight weeks participants performed a bout of 10 × 10 eccentric-emphasised leg extensions. Outcome measures included quadriceps maximal voluntary contraction (MVC), muscle soreness, creatine kinase (CK) and inflammation (Interleukin-6, high-sensitive C-reactive protein; CRP) assessed at baseline and post-exercise.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>EIMD symptoms such as muscle soreness and function were modest and consistent with previous reports in older adults. Overall, n-3 PUFA supplementation did not improve functional recovery. However, a borderline greater MVC loss was observed in the n-3 PUFA group (time × group: P = .064), which resulted from significantly lower MVC in the n-3 PUFA group at 24 h (difference: −10.9%, 95%CI: −21.4;−0.40%, P = .042) and at 72 h (difference: −9.80, 95%CI: −18.3;−1.27, P = .025) post-exercise compared to the placebo. No significant overall group differences were observed for CK, interleukin-6, CRP, but CK concentrations significantly increased from baseline at 24 h post-exercise in the placebo group (change: +81.1%, 95%CI:10.5;152%, P = .014). Habitual physical activity and sex emerged as significant moderators of molecular recovery in an exploratory analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>n-3 PUFA supplementation did not improve functional recovery, but different molecular response patterns were observed. Habitual physical activity and sex may be determinants of post-exercise response; this exploratory finding warrants confirmation in larger studies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Eight-week omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation alters but does not attenuate exercise-induced muscle damage in older adults: a randomised controlled trial

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Home hospital has been shown to achieve comparable, if not better, clinical and patient-centred outcomes compared to brick-and-mortar (BAM) hospitalisation. Family caregivers (FCs) play an essential role in delivering home hospital care; however, their perceptions towards the home hospital model remain an active area of inquiry, particularly in rural settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a mixed methods analysis of FCs of patients participating in a multicenter randomised controlled trial of rural home hospital in the USA and Canada. We compared pre- and post-intervention burden among home hospital and BAM caregivers with the Zarit Burden Interview-12 (ZBI-12) scale (n = 20 home hospital, n = 10 BAM). We conducted semi-structured qualitative interviews with home hospital caregivers (n = 19). Qualitative data were coded and analysed using thematic analysis to construct core themes and subthemes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>There was no significant difference in median ZBI-12 scores between home hospital and BAM at admission (4 interquartile range [IQR 2–9.3] vs 5 [IQR 0.3–9.3]; P = .723), discharge (6 [3.3–8] vs 7.5 [2.5–11.8], P = .309), or change from admission to discharge (0 [−2.5 to 3] vs 1.5 [0–3.5]; P = .269). Our qualitative analysis revealed three central themes: (i) The caregiving experience was positively shaped by strong communication and shared decision-making with the care team; (ii) Caregivers described receiving high-quality home hospital care, particularly surrounding patient-centeredness and technology; and (iii) Home hospital was perceived to offer greater flexibility, comfort and psychosocial support compared to BAM hospitalisation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Home hospital provides numerous benefits for FCs without increasing perceived burden; further work is needed to establish potential supports to optimise their experience.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The experience of family caregivers when their loved one is home hospitalized: a mixed methods analysis of a randomized controlled trial

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Interprofessional training is essential for high-quality care of older adults. Despite widespread recognition of its importance, evidence on perceived geriatric competence remains limited to studies on single countries or professions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Secondary analysis of a COST Action multinational multilingual web-based survey (PROmoting GeRiAtric Medicine in countries where it is still eMergING, PROGRAMMING) conducted across the 27 European Union Member States (EU-27) and non-EU-27 countries between 9 October 2023 and 5 June 2024. Four thousand seven hundred eighty-eight professionals from 10 core health and social care groups were included. We explored perceived Knowledge, Relevance and Interest across seven domains required for comprehensive geriatric assessment: frailty, falls and mobility, delirium, depression, mild cognitive impairment and dementia screening, nutritional assessment and malnutrition, polypharmacy and deprescribing. Student’s t test; one-way analysis of variance, hierarchical clustering and latent class analysis were used to identify interprofessional differences and shared patterns across professions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Mean age was 42.4 years (SD 11.9); 3432 (71.7%) were women; 2893 (60.4%) worked in EU-27 countries. Interprofessional differences were observed across all topics. Physiotherapists led in falls and mobility (mean 4.21, SD 0.75), pharmacists in polypharmacy and deprescribing (mean 3.51, SD 1.07), and psychologists/psychotherapists in depression (mean 3.96, SD 0.82). A medical doctors–nurses–pharmacists cluster emerged for Knowledge and Interest; 34.4% pharmacists fell in the low relevance class. Social workers and speech and language therapists showed a low Knowledge–high Interest mismatch. EU-27 professionals reported higher scores than non-EU-27 professionals across most topics (P &lt; .001).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Perceived knowledge, relevance and interest showed substantial variation across professions and regions, while revealing shared professional profiles. This may inform team-based interprofessional education.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Profiling perceived knowledge, relevance and interest across geriatric topics of health and social care professionals: multinational electronic cross-sectional survey

                    <jats:p>The comorbidity of pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) and diabetes mellitus (DM) is rising among adults aged ≥ 65 years in China. <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Postoperative sleep disturbance (PSD) is a common disorder among elderly patients undergoing surgery and is associated with a higher risk of adverse outcomes. This meta-analysis investigated the effects of esketamine on postoperative sleep quality among elderly patients.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>PubMed, Embase, The Cochrane Library, CNKI, and Wanfang databases were searched to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing intravenous esketamine with control in elderly patients (≥ 60 years) undergoing elective surgery in general anesthesia. Sleep quality on postoperative day (POD) 1 was the primary outcome. Other outcomes included sleep quality at other time points, objective sleep parameters, pain, cognitive function, and adverse events.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Seventeen RCTs involving 2587 patients were included. Regarding the primary outcome, esketamine significantly improved subjective sleep quality on POD 1 (SMD = -0.72; 95% CI, -1.10 to -0.34; I² = 93%), POD 2 (SMD = -1.40; 95% CI, -2.15 to -0.64; I² = 97%), and POD 7 (SMD = -0.38; 95% CI, -0.62 to -0.14; I² = 53%). Objective sleep measures on POD 1 revealed longer total sleep time, reduced sleep latency, and improved sleep efficiency. Esketamine also decreased pain intensity (SMD = -0.63; 95% CI, -0.88 to -0.38; I² = 70%) and improved MMSE scores (SMD = 0.65; 95% CI, 0.42 to 0.89; I² = 0%). Esketamine was associated with a lower risk of nausea or vomiting. No significant differences was observed between the two groups in terms of dizziness, while hypotension occurred less frequently with esketamine.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among elderly surgical patients, perioperative esketamine was associated with improved postoperative sleep quality, reduced pain intensity, and a potential improvement in cognitive function, without a significant increase in the risk of major adverse events. However, high-quality RCTs are needed to confirm these findings and determine optimal dosing regimens. Of note, all 17 included trials were conducted in China, potentially limiting the generalizability of our findings to other populations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Effects of esketamine on postoperative sleep quality in elderly patients under general anesthesia: a systematic review and meta-analysis

records.abstract: <jats:p>Introduction: Sarcopenia, an age-related syndrome characterized by progressive loss of muscle mass, decreased muscle strength, and/or reduced physical performance, is associated with disruptions in amino acid and lipid metabolism. This study aimed to investigate serum metabolic alterations associated with sarcopenia in older adults. Methods: In this cross-sectional study, 50 patients with sarcopenia (diagnosed per 2014 AWGS criteria) were matched 1:1 by age and sex with non-sarcopenic controls from a pool of 2,965 individuals. Assessments included skeletal muscle mass, grip strength, and gait speed. Serum metabolomic profiling was conducted using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS). The screening of differential metabolites: variable importance in the projection (VIP) > 1 derived from the OPLS-DA model, and adjusted p-value based on false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05 calculated by two-sample t-test. Results: Among 100 participants aged 60–87 years, individuals with sarcopenia showed significantly lower BMI, grip strength, albumin, and ASMI than controls (all p < 0.05), whereas lipid levels were comparable. PCA suggested weak group separation, whereas PLS-DA achieved clearer discrimination by sex and sarcopenia status. Differential metabolites identified in the sarcopenia group included arginine, leucine and histidinyl-histidine, the latter of which exhibited decreased abundance. Concomitant alterations in the levels of lipid metabolites collectively suggest disrupted amino acid and lipid metabolism. Conclusion: Patterns of dysregulated amino acid and fatty acid metabolism were observed in older adults with sarcopenia. Such metabolic disturbances might serve as candidate biomarkers to inform early detection and nutritional intervention strategies.</jats:p>
title: Serum Metabolomic Profiling Reveals Disrupted Amino Acid and Fatty Acid Metabolism in Older Adults with Sarcopenia

records.abstract: <jats:p>Background The heterogeneity within the group of older women challenges balancing overtreatment and undertreatment. The tumor-stroma ratio (TSR) has emerged as a potential prognostic marker. In this study, the prognostic value of the TSR in older women with breast cancer is investigated. Methods Women aged ≥70 years, diagnosed between 2003-2009 with hormone receptor-positive (HR+), human epidermal growth factor 2 (HER2)-negative breast cancer were included, excluding those treated with chemotherapy or neoadjuvant therapy. Results Altogether, 2,974 women were included: 70% had a stroma-low tumor and 30% stroma-high. The likelihood of having a stroma-high tumor increased with age (p = 0.021). Univariable analyses presented worse overall survival (OS; HR 1.106, 95% CI 1.016-1.204, p = 0.020) and unfavorable metastasis-free period (MFP; HR 1.324, 95% CI 1.044-1.680, p = 0.021) in stroma-high patients, but this was not significant in multivariable analyses (OS: p = 0.080, MFP: p = 0.961). In multivariable analyses, the TSR remained prognostic regarding OS in women without relevant comorbidities (HR 1.376, 95% CI 1.144-1.655, p < 0.001), and with a ductal carcinoma and no adjuvant systemic therapy (HR 1.455, 95% CI 1.114-1.900, p = 0.006). Conclusion High stromal content was associated with worse OS and MFP and was especially an independent, unfavorable prognostic factor in patients without relevant comorbidities, and those with a ductal carcinoma and no adjuvant therapy. In these specific patient groups, the TSR could support further personalization of treatment, such as de-escalating therapy in those with favorable prognosis (stroma-low) or by treating those with an unfavorable prognosis (stroma-high) more aggressively.</jats:p>
title: The Prognostic Value of the Tumor-Stroma Ratio (TSR) is Most Pronounced in Older Breast Cancer Patients without Relevant Comorbidities
